results.proposed_proof:
**Given:** The diagram algebra, link-state bases, $q,\delta$, and reflection conventions.

[F1] Diagram stacking is associative, reflection is an anti-involution, the elementary diagrams $d_i$ generate, and $d_i^2=\delta d_i$, $d_id_{i\pm1}d_i=d_i$, $d_id_j=d_jd_i$ for $|i-j|>1$ ([[thm-temperley-lieb-diagram-category-laws]], [[thm-temperley-lieb-diagram-generators-span]], [[lem-temperley-lieb-generators-satisfy-local-relations]]). The spanning Jones normal forms are [[thm-temperley-lieb-generator-normal-form]].

[F2] The link-state action and rightmost-site restriction sequence are [[lem-temperley-lieb-link-state-module-action-is-well-defined]] and [[lem-temperley-lieb-link-state-restriction-filtration]].

[F3] For generic $q$ the link-state Gram matrix is invertible, by [[lem-temperley-lieb-link-state-gram-determinant]]. The elementary rank-one diagram identity then makes each standard simple: a nonzero vector paired with $y$ is sent to any prescribed $x$ by the diagram with halves $x,y$.

[F4] Criticality and adjacent reflection labels are those of [[def-temperley-lieb-complex-critical-labels-and-reflection]].



**Proof technique:** Use an explicit partial closure of braid words, the induced link-state basis, and adjunction.

1.1 It suffices to perform computations for left modules: send a right module to the left module with $a\cdot v=v\cdot a^*$, where $*$ is diagram reflection. This is an exact equivalence preserving Hom direction, induction and restriction. Fix a square root of $q$ and put $g_i=q^{1/2}1-q^{-1/2}d_i$. Expanding with [F1] gives $g_i^{-1}=q^{-1/2}1-q^{1/2}d_i$ and $g_ig_{i+1}g_i=g_{i+1}g_ig_{i+1}$. Let $T_n:A_{n+1}\to A_n$ close the last top endpoint to the last bottom endpoint externally on the right, removing any resulting loop with factor $\delta$. This is an $A_n$-bimodule map by the matching rule. Define $M_n=g_n\cdots g_2g_1^2g_2\cdots g_n$ and $F_n=T_n(M_n)$; set $F_0=\delta$. Every summand of $M_n$ has an even total number of square-root factors, so $F_n$ has coefficients in $\mathbb Z[q,q^{-1}]$, independent of the chosen square root. [F1, given, construct, algebra]

1.2 For clarity give a basis proof of the induction sequence. In left-module notation put $h_r=d_rd_{r+1}\cdots d_n$ for $1\le r\le n$, and $h_{n+1}=1$. A state $d$ is $r$-admissible when it has no adjacent arc at an index $i\ge r$. The tensors $h_r\otimes d$ with $d$ $r$-admissible, including all $1\otimes d$, span $A_{n+1}\otimes_{A_n}V_{n,p}$. First, a diagram word is a sum of $h_ru$ with $u\in A_n$: reverse a spanning Jones normal form from [F1]. Its initial ascending block is either $h_r$ or contains no $d_n$, and every later block lies in $A_n$. The surjection from the presented algebra to the diagram algebra is supplied by the local relations, so this spanning assertion applies to diagram words. Next, if $d$ has its largest adjacent arc at $s\ge r$, write $d=d_sf$. For $n\ge3$ this can be done without division: move the endpoint immediately outside that adjacent arc through the arc, so applying $d_s$ restores $d$ and creates no loop. If $s=1$ use site $3$; otherwise use site $s-1$. The outside site is either a defect or an endpoint of another arc, and reconnecting its former partner supplies the inverse state $f$. Now the relations give $h_r\otimes d=h_{s+2}\otimes d_r\cdots d_{s-1}d$. The latter state is $(s+2)$-admissible: the adjacent arc at $s$ has moved to $r$, all intervening endpoints shift by two, and the tail beyond $s+1$ still has no adjacent arc. Repetition, increasing $r$, proves spanning. At $n=1,2$ the same conclusion is checked on the at most two states, except $n=2,p=1,\delta=0$, when the needed factorization $d=d_1f$ fails. [F1, F2, given, construct, algebra]

2.1 The braid relations give $g_iM_n=M_ng_i$ for $i<n$. To see this directly, commute $g_i$ past all $g_j$ with $|j-i|>1$ in the descending and ascending strings; the remaining equality is $g_ig_{i+1}g_i=g_{i+1}g_ig_{i+1}$ on each side of the middle string. This proves the equality inductively in the length of the strings, starting with $g_1g_2g_1^2g_2=g_2g_1^2g_2g_1$. Bimodule linearity of $T_n$ gives $g_iF_n=F_ng_i$, hence $d_iF_n=F_nd_i$. Thus $F_n$ is central. Reversing the palindromic word $M_n$ and reflecting its closure leaves it unchanged, so $F_n^*=F_n$. [F1, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Compute $F_n$ on the state $z_p$ with adjacent arcs $(1,2),(3,4),\ldots,(2p-1,2p)$ and all remaining sites defects. At a cup, expansion of the two adjacent crossings uses the identities $d_ig_{i+1}g_i=-d_id_{i+1}$ and $g_ig_{i+1}d_i=-d_{i+1}d_i$; for example the first is $qd_i-d_id_{i+1}-\delta d_i+q^{-1}d_id_{i+1}d_i=-d_id_{i+1}$. The two minus signs on the two sides of each cup cancel. Thus each initial cup can be removed without changing the coefficient of $z_p$. For the $t=n-2p$ defect strands, expand the auxiliary strand successively from its first crossing. A smoothing connecting two defects vanishes in the standard quotient. There are two remaining continuations: following the auxiliary strand on its two sides gives respectively $q^t\delta-q^{t-1}=q^{t+1}$ and $q^{-t}\delta-q^{-t+1}=q^{-(t+1)}$. The factors arise by choosing the identity smoothing at each subsequent crossing until the final cap; that cap either closes a loop or chooses the second smoothing, giving the displayed two terms on each side. Hence the coefficient of $z_p$ is $f_{n,p}$. For generic $q$, centrality and [F3] make $F_n$ scalar on the entire standard: over $\mathbb C$ a central operator has an eigenvalue, whose nonzero eigenspace is the simple module. Since the action matrices and $f_{n,p}$ are Laurent polynomial in $q$, this scalar identity extends to every $q\ne0$. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 On the submodule and quotient in [F2], $F_{n-1}$ acts by $f_{n-1,p}$ and $f_{n-1,p-1}$. Their difference is $(q-q^{-1})(q^{n-2p+1}-q^{-(n-2p+1)})$. Under the noncritical and $q\ne\pm1$ hypotheses it is nonzero. The operator on the restriction satisfies $(F_{n-1}-f_{n-1,p})(F_{n-1}-f_{n-1,p-1})=0$, because each factor kills its respective subquotient. Its two spectral projections therefore give an invariant direct sum splitting the restriction sequence. [F2, F4, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 Append an adjacent arc at sites $n+1,n+2$ to $d$, obtaining $\bar d\in V_{n+2,p+1}$. The map $\Phi(u\otimes d)=u\bar d$ into $V_{n+2,p+1}\downarrow$ is balanced and $A_{n+1}$-linear: elements of $A_n$ act only on the first $n$ sites. Its image of $h_r\otimes d$ has its rightmost adjacent arc at $r$; deleting that arc recovers $d$. Conversely every $(n+2,p+1)$-state has a rightmost adjacent arc; delete it at position $r$, and the remaining state is $r$-admissible. These two operations are inverse, so the spanning tensors in step 1.2 map bijectively to the link-state basis. They are therefore a basis and $\Phi$ is an isomorphism, except in the stated exceptional case. Applying the restriction sequence [F2] to $V_{n+2,p+1}$ now gives the asserted induction sequence. Applying step 4.1 at rank $n+2$ splits it whenever $(n,p)$ is noncritical, since $n+2-2(p+1)+1=n-2p+1$. [F1, F2, step 4.1, step 1.2, algebra]

6.1 Suppose $(n,p)$ is critical, $q\ne\pm1$, and $z_p$ is as in step 3.1. In the induced basis the coefficient of $h_{2p+1}\otimes z_p$ in $F_{n+1}(1\otimes z_p)$ is $(-1)^n(\delta^2-4)\ne0.$ Here is the local expansion computing it. First take $p=0$. To leave $h_1=d_1\cdots d_n$ after reduction, the first pair of crossings of the closed auxiliary strand has three contributing smoothings, with weights $-1,-1,\delta q^{-1}$; the fourth, of weight $q$, closes off the needed through path. This gives $-2+\delta q^{-1}$. At each of the next $n-1$ pairs exactly one continuation retains the required external matching, of weight $-1$: the other continuation either caps the auxiliary path prematurely or makes an additional bottom arc. At the final pair the corresponding three weights are $-1,-1,\delta q$, giving $-2+\delta q$. Their product is $(-1)^{n-1}(-2+\delta q^{-1})(-2+\delta q)=(-1)^n(\delta^2-4)$. These connectivity conditions simply track the path beginning at the first top endpoint and ending at the last bottom endpoint; all other endpoints of $h_1$ are adjacent pairs, so any premature cap is excluded. For $p>0$, remove the first $p$ cups using the two local identities in step 3.1, on both sides of the auxiliary path. This leaves the same computation on $n-2p$ sites; $n-2p>0$ by criticality and $\kappa\ge2$, and its parity equals that of $n$. The target basis tensor is $h_{2p+1}\otimes z_p=h_1\otimes z_p$, by successive $d_id_{i+1}d_i=d_i$ reductions. One may do the cup removal first for $\delta\ne0$ by inserting $\delta^{-1}d_{2j-1}$ at each initial cup. The resulting coefficient identity extends to $\delta=0$: the induced basis reduction in step 1.2 uses no division, so its matrices, and this coefficient, are Laurent polynomials in $q$. Finally $\delta^2-4=(q-q^{-1})^2\ne0$. [F1, F4, step 1.1, step 3.1, step 1.2, step 5.1, algebra]

7.1 In the induction sequence at a critical $(n,p)$ the two standard constituents have the same eigenvalue $f=f_{n+1,p}=f_{n+1,p+1}$. The central endomorphism $F_{n+1}-f$ kills both constituents but is nonzero on the induction by step 6.1. Consequently it factors through the quotient $V_{n+1,p}$ into the submodule $V_{n+1,p+1}$, giving a nonzero map between these adjacent reflected standards. Explicitly, lift a quotient vector to the induction, apply $F_{n+1}-f$, and use the inverse of the submodule injection; the result is independent of the lift because this operator kills the submodule. [F4, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 5.1, step 6.1, construct]

8.1 Every symmetric pair has the form $(n+j,p),(n+j,p+j)$ for a critical $(n,p)$ and $1\le j<\kappa$. For $j\ge2$, induction and restriction at the noncritical labels give $\operatorname{Hom}(V_{n+j,p},V_{n+j,p+j})\cong\operatorname{Hom}(V_{n+j-1,p}\uparrow,V_{n+j,p+j})\cong\operatorname{Hom}(V_{n+j-1,p},V_{n+j,p+j}\downarrow)\cong\operatorname{Hom}(V_{n+j-1,p},V_{n+j-1,p+j-1}).$ In the first and last isomorphisms the extra standard summand has a different $F$-eigenvalue: substitute $q^{2(n-2p+1)}=1$ in step 3.1, and equality would force $j=1$ or $j=\kappa$. Thus its Hom is zero. The middle adjunction is explicit: $f\mapsto(v\mapsto f(1\otimes v))$, with inverse $g\mapsto(a\otimes v\mapsto ag(v))$. This works also when an extraneous summand is out of range. Reducing $j$ to $1$ and applying step 7.1 proves nonvanishing for every reflected pair. Returning along step 1.1 gives all statements for the repository's right modules. [F4, step 1.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, step 5.1, step 7.1, algebra] ∎

**Given:** $q,\kappa\ge2$, the standard modules, their capping forms and the label convention.

[F1] The central spectral projections give the split restriction for noncritical labels ([[lem-temperley-lieb-annular-central-element-and-reflection-maps]]).

[F2] The generic orthogonal restriction calculation gives $G_{n,p}=U^{\mathsf T}(G_{n-1,p}\oplus\alpha G_{n-1,p-1})U$ with $U$ unitriangular and $\alpha=[n-2p+2]_q/[n-2p+1]_q$; its full local block computation is in [[lem-temperley-lieb-link-state-gram-determinant]].

[F3] Critical forms are nondegenerate ([[lem-temperley-lieb-critical-standard-modules-are-simple]]). The form is symmetric and invariant ([[lem-temperley-lieb-link-state-gram-form-is-invariant]]).

[F4] $\dim V_{n,p}=\dim V_{n-1,p}+\dim V_{n-1,p-1}$ ([[thm-temperley-lieb-link-state-dimension-formula]]). Reflection is as in [[def-temperley-lieb-complex-critical-labels-and-reflection]].



**Proof technique:** Specialize a regular orthogonal splitting, then compare the two dimension recursions.

1.1 At a noncritical root, the two eigenvalues used for [F1] differ by $(q-q^{-1})(q^{n-2p+1}-q^{-(n-2p+1)})\ne0$. The spectral projector onto the rightmost-defect summand is $(F_{n-1}-f_{n-1,p-1})/(f_{n-1,p}-f_{n-1,p-1})$. Its entries are rational functions regular at the root; subtracting this projection from each standard quotient lift gives a unitriangular splitting matrix $U$, also regular there. Since $F_{n-1}^*=F_{n-1}$ and the eigenvalues differ, the two summands are orthogonal. For generic $q$ this is exactly the orthogonal splitting of [F2], since the submodule form is nondegenerate and its orthogonal complement is unique. Thus the matrix identity in [F2] is an identity of rational matrices regular at every noncritical root, and specializes there. This continuity argument applies to the entire matrix identity, rather than inferring a rank from a specialized determinant. If $n=2p$, there is only the quotient summand and direct capping gives $G_{2p,p}=\delta G_{2p-1,p-1}$, the same formula with $\alpha=[2]/[1]=\delta$. [F1, F2, F3, given, algebra]

2.1 Since $\kappa\ge2$, $q\ne\pm1$; hence $[a]_q=0$ precisely when $\kappa\mid a$. At a noncritical label the denominator of $\alpha$ is nonzero and its numerator vanishes precisely when $r=\kappa-1$. The kernel dimension of the specialized block form in step 1.1 is therefore $\dim R_{n-1,p}+\dim V_{n-1,p-1}$ in that case, and $\dim R_{n-1,p}+\dim R_{n-1,p-1}$ otherwise. Critical labels give zero by [F3]; the all-defect form is $(1)$, giving $R_{n,0}=0$. Subtraction from [F4] gives the companion recursion: $\dim L_{n,p}=\dim V_{n,p}$ at critical labels; at noncritical labels it is $\dim L_{n-1,p}$ if $r=\kappa-1$, and $\dim L_{n-1,p}+\dim L_{n-1,p-1}$ otherwise. [F2, F3, F4, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Prove the reflected-dimension formula by induction on $n$, with out-of-range labels assigned dimension zero. Write $a=p+r-\kappa$. If $r\notin\{1,\kappa-1\}$, neither predecessor is critical. Their reflection indices are respectively $a-1$ and $a$, so induction and step 2.1 give $\dim R_{n,p}=\dim L_{n-1,a-1}+\dim L_{n-1,a}$. The reflected label $a$ has remainder $\kappa-r$, which is also neither $1$ nor $\kappa-1$; its companion recursion gives exactly $\dim L_{n,a}$. [F4, step 2.1, algebra]

3.2 When $\kappa=2$, every noncritical label has $r=1=\kappa-1$ and both predecessors are critical. The radical recursion gives $\dim R_{n,p}=\dim V_{n-1,p-1}=\dim L_{n-1,p-1}$. Since $a=p-1$ and the companion recursion at $(n,a)$ also has remainder $1$, this is $\dim L_{n,a}$. The same formula holds for $n=2p$: it gives $\dim R_{2p,p}=\dim V_{2p-1,p-1}=\dim V_{2p,p}$, as required by the identically zero form. [F3, F4, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 If $r=\kappa-1$ and $\kappa>2$, the predecessor $(n-1,p-1)$ is critical, while $(n-1,p)$ has reflected index $a-1$. Consequently $\dim R_{n,p}=\dim L_{n-1,a-1}+\dim V_{n-1,p-1}$. Here $a=p-1$, and criticality gives $V_{n-1,p-1}=L_{n-1,a}$. The companion recursion at $(n,a)$ has remainder $1\ne\kappa-1$, so this sum is $\dim L_{n,a}$. If $r=1$ and $\kappa>2$, $(n-1,p)$ is critical and its radical is zero; the reflection of $(n-1,p-1)$ has index $a$. Thus $\dim R_{n,p}=\dim L_{n-1,a}$. The reflected label at rank $n$ has remainder $\kappa-1$, whose companion recursion is precisely $\dim L_{n,a}=\dim L_{n-1,a}$. [F3, F4, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 The initial $p=0$ case has $a<0$ and zero radical. All predecessor terms whose indices leave the allowed range are zero. In particular the recursions in steps 3.1–3.3 give zero when $a<0$; when $a=0$ they use the initial all-defect dimension $1$. These boundary rules also cover $n=0,1$. The induction establishes the stated formula for present reflected labels and the zero radical for absent labels. [F4, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, step 3.2, algebra] ∎

**Given:** The complex standards and the above arc-label notation; an allowed label has $0\le p\le\lfloor n/2\rfloor$.

[F1] Nonzero cell-form quotients are absolutely simple, pairwise distinct, exhaustive, and their form radicals are unique maximal submodules ([[cor-temperley-lieb-nonzero-cell-forms-classify-simple-modules]]).

[F2] There is a nonzero map $V_{n,a}\to V_{n,p}$ for every adjacent reflected pair $a<p$ ([[lem-temperley-lieb-annular-central-element-and-reflection-maps]]).

[F3] The corresponding dimensions satisfy $\dim R_{n,p}=\dim L_{n,a}$, or zero if $a$ is absent ([[lem-temperley-lieb-root-gram-rank-and-reflection-dimensions]]).

[F4] Critical standards are simple with nondegenerate form; at $\delta=0$ the positive-rank perfect-matching standard is simple despite its zero ordinary form ([[lem-temperley-lieb-critical-standard-modules-are-simple]], [[lem-temperley-lieb-zero-loop-perfect-matching-standard-module-is-simple]]).

[F5] Capping is the invariant Gram pairing, and a diagram with halves $x,y$ acts on its own standard by $z\mapsto\phi(y,z)x$; its propagation number is that standard's defect number ([[lem-temperley-lieb-link-state-gram-form-is-invariant]]).

[F6] The Gram determinant is a product of nonvanishing quantum-integer quotients when $\kappa=\infty$ ([[lem-temperley-lieb-link-state-gram-determinant]]).



**Proof technique:** Compare the kernel and image of a reflection map with the exact Gram-radical dimensions.

1.1 The form is nonzero unless $\delta=0$ and the positive-rank defect number is zero. Indeed, when $\delta\ne0$ a state's pairing with itself is $\delta^p\ne0$. When $\delta=0$ and $t=n-2p>0$, take $x$ with arcs $(1,2),(3,4),\ldots,(2p-1,2p)$ and $y$ with arcs $(2,3),(4,5),\ldots,(2p,2p+1)$; all other sites are defects. Their overlay on sites $1,\ldots,2p+1$ is one open alternating path, with no cycle, and all remaining defect paths match. Thus $\phi(x,y)=1$. If $p=0$ the form is $(1)$. For $t=0,n>0$, every overlay has a closed component and hence value zero at $\delta=0$. Consequently [F1] applies to exactly the stated nonexceptional labels. [F1, F5, given, construct]

2.1 More strongly, any submodule not contained in the form radical is the entire standard. If $z$ lies outside the radical, choose $y$ with $\phi(y,z)=1$. For any vector $x$, the diagram with halves $x,y$ sends $z$ to $x$ by [F5]; hence $z$ generates the standard. Also, if $p>p'$ and the source form is nonzero, every map between any quotients of $V_{n,p}$ and $V_{n,p'}$ is zero. Choose $y,z$ in the source with $\phi(y,z)=1$. A diagram with halves $x,y$ has $n-2p<n-2p'$ propagating strands and therefore acts as zero on the target and its quotients. Applying a proposed homomorphism to its action on the class of $z$ gives zero on the class of every $x$, hence the map is zero. [F5, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

3.1 Consider an adjacent reflected pair $a<p$ and a nonzero $f:V_{n,a}\to V_{n,p}$ from [F2]. Its kernel is proper and therefore lies in $R_{n,a}$ by step 2.1. Its image also lies in $R_{n,p}$: otherwise step 2.1 makes $f$ surjective, and its inverse isomorphism $V_{n,p}\to V_{n,a}/\ker f$ contradicts the quotient-vanishing assertion in step 2.1. The source is never the zero-form exceptional label, since $a<p$. If the target is the exceptional label, its simplicity in [F4] instead gives $\operatorname{im}f=V_{n,p}=R_{n,p}$ directly. Thus in every case $\ker f\subseteq R_{n,a}$ and $\operatorname{im}f\subseteq R_{n,p}$. [F2, F4, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Rank-nullity and [F3] now force equality in both inclusions: $\dim V_{n,a}=\dim\ker f+\dim\operatorname{im}f\le\dim R_{n,a}+\dim R_{n,p}=\dim R_{n,a}+\dim L_{n,a}=\dim V_{n,a}$. Therefore $\ker f=R_{n,a}$ and $\operatorname{im}f=R_{n,p}\cong L_{n,a}$, which is simple by [F1]. For an absent reflected label [F3] gives $R_{n,p}=0$. At a critical label [F4] gives the same. [F1, F3, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 For a nonexceptional standard, steps 2.1 and 4.1 show every proper submodule is contained in a radical which is zero or simple. Thus its only submodules are $0,R,V$ and every quotient is indecomposable. When the radical is nonzero, the exact radical/head sequence cannot split: a complementary submodule would be proper and not contained in the radical, contradicting step 2.1. It has exactly the two displayed simple factors. The critical $\kappa=1$ branch is [F4]. If $\kappa=\infty$, no quantum integer in the determinant vanishes, so the determinant and hence the form are nondegenerate; this is [F6]. Exhaustion and distinction of the nonzero heads are [F1]. [F1, F3, F4, F6, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 4.1, algebra]

6.1 At $\delta=0$ and $n=2p>0$, $\kappa=2$ and the reflected arc label is $p-1$. Step 1.1 identifies the form radical as all of $V_{2p,p}$, while step 4.1 identifies it with $L_{2p,p-1}$. This agrees with the separately proved actual simplicity [F4]; its zero form quotient introduces no extra simple label. The remaining standards have nonzero forms and hence the complete simple labels are $0,\ldots,p-1$. Finally, each noncritical standard shares factors only with its adjacent reflection neighbors by step 4.1, and every present neighbor occurs. Taking the equivalence generated by these edges gives precisely the stated reflection chains. A critical head occurs only in its own simple standard, giving singleton classes. [F1, F3, F4, step 1.1, step 4.1, step 5.1, algebra] ∎

**Given:** The complex standards, their arc labels, and ordinary form radicals $R_{n,p}$.

[F1] Each nonexceptional standard has unique simple head $L_{n,p}$ and zero or simple radical; a nonzero radical is the head at its adjacent reflected label. These nonzero heads are pairwise distinct. At $\delta=0,n=2m>0$, $V_{2m,m}=R_{2m,m}\cong L_{2m,m-1}$ is simple and $L_{2m,m}=0$ ([[lem-temperley-lieb-root-noncritical-radicals-and-simple-heads]]).

[F2] Adjacent-reflection maps exist, and the central element is scalar on each standard ([[lem-temperley-lieb-annular-central-element-and-reflection-maps]]).

[F3] The rank-one diagram identity is $z\cdot C_{y,x}=\phi(y,z)x$ ([[lem-temperley-lieb-link-state-gram-form-is-invariant]]).

[F4] Endomorphisms of an absolutely simple finite-dimensional complex module are scalar ([[thm-schurs-lemma-for-modules]]); the link-state dimension is the ballot number ([[thm-temperley-lieb-link-state-dimension-formula]]).



**Proof technique:** Use the complete submodule lists and the rank-one operators.

1.1 If the form of $V_{n,p}$ is nonzero, choose $y,z$ with $\phi(y,z)=1$. For an endomorphism $h$, [F3] gives $h(x)=h(z\cdot C_{y,x})=h(z)\cdot C_{y,x}=\phi(y,h(z))x$ for every $x$. Thus $h$ is scalar. In the exceptional zero-form case the module itself is simple by [F1], so [F4] gives the same conclusion. This proves every diagonal dimension is one. [F1, F3, F4, given, choose, algebra]

1.2 It remains to include $Z=V_{2m,m}$ at $\delta=0$. Here $Z\cong L_{2m,m-1}$ is simple by [F1]. For a nonexceptional source $V_{2m,p}$, a map to $Z$ has simple image; if nonzero it is a simple quotient of the source, hence its head $L_{2m,p}$. Distinctness of the labels forces $p=m-1$, in which case [F2] supplies a map and [F4] gives uniqueness. This is exactly the adjacent-reflection case. [F1, F2, F4, algebra]

2.1 Suppose both source and target have nonzero forms and $p>p'$. The rank-one operators for the source have $n-2p<n-2p'$ propagating strands and kill the target. Choosing $y,z$ as in step 1.1, a proposed homomorphism $h$ therefore satisfies $h(x)=h(z\cdot C_{y,x})=h(z)\cdot C_{y,x}=0$. Hence the Hom space is zero. [F3, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Suppose both forms are nonzero and $p<p'$. A nonzero map cannot be surjective: its inverse quotient isomorphism would contradict step 2.1, whose proof also applies to quotients of the target. Thus its image lies in the simple radical $R_{n,p'}$. The kernel is a proper submodule of the source and hence is $0$ or $R_{n,p}$. If it is zero, the source is simple because it embeds into the simple radical. In either case the image is isomorphic to the source head $L_{n,p}$. By [F1] and distinction of simple labels this is possible exactly when $p$ is the adjacent reflected label of $p'$. Such a map exists by [F2]; it factors as the head quotient followed by an isomorphism $L_{n,p}\cong R_{n,p'}$ and the radical inclusion. Schur's lemma makes this factorization unique up to scalar, so its Hom space has dimension one and the stated kernel and image. If the target radical is zero there is no such map. [F1, F2, F4, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 A nonzero map from $Z$ to $V_{2m,p'}$, $p'<m$, is injective. If its image is the radical, [F1] makes it $L_{2m,p'-1}$; this cannot equal $L_{2m,m-1}$ because $p'-1<m-1$. Otherwise its image is the entire target by the submodule list in [F1], so the target is simple. At $\kappa=2$ every $1\le p'<m$ has a present reflected label $p'-1$ with a nonzero head, hence is reducible; thus $p'=0$. That standard is one-dimensional. The exceptional module has dimension $\frac1{m+1}\binom{2m}{m}$ by [F4], which is greater than one for $m\ge2$: there are at least the distinct matchings with initial arcs $(1,2)$ and $(1,2m)$. Equality therefore occurs only at $m=1$. In that case both $V_{2,1}$ and $V_{2,0}$ are one-dimensional, and $d_1$ acts by zero on each, giving the stated isomorphism and one-dimensional Hom. These cases exhaust all labels, including rank zero. [F1, F4, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

**Given:** The complex diagram algebra, its standards and simple heads, with ordinary zero-form quotient labels retained.

[F1] The complete standard composition factors and their exceptional zero-loop convention are [[lem-temperley-lieb-root-noncritical-radicals-and-simple-heads]]. The nonzero heads are self-dual for the duality induced by diagram reflection: their nondegenerate quotient forms identify them with their twisted linear duals.

[F2] The cellular diagram basis gives a filtration by two-sided ideals of diagrams with at most a given number of propagating strands. Its layer at defect label $t=n-2s$ is the bimodule $U_s\otimes_{\mathbb C}V_{n,s}$, where $U_s$ is the left module obtained from $V_{n,s}$ by reflection ([[thm-temperley-lieb-link-state-diagram-basis-is-cellular]]).

[F3] Finite-dimensional modules over finite-dimensional algebras have projective covers, unique up to isomorphism over the target ([[thm-projective-covers-exist-and-are-unique-for-finite-dimensional-algebras]]), applied also to the opposite algebra for right modules. A cover has a superfluous kernel.

[F4] The central $F_n$, its standard eigenvalues and the induction sequences are [[lem-temperley-lieb-annular-central-element-and-reflection-maps]].

[F5] A simple complex module has scalar endomorphisms ([[thm-schurs-lemma-for-modules]]).



**Proof technique:** Apply a primitive projective summand to the cellular bimodule filtration, and identify the repeated-induction realization by its two extremal standard constituents.

1.1 Fix a nonzero head $L=L_{n,p}$ and its finite-dimensional projective cover $\pi:P\to L$ from [F3]. Since $L$ is cyclic, choose a surjection $\alpha:A_n\to L$. Projectivity of $P$ and of the finite free module $A_n$ gives maps $s:P\to A_n$ and $t:A_n\to P$ with $\alpha s=\pi$ and $\pi t=\alpha$. Then $\pi ts=\pi$. Consequently $P=ts(P)+\ker\pi$; superfluity gives $ts(P)=P$, so $ts$ is invertible by finite dimensionality. Replacing $s$ by $s(ts)^{-1}$ makes $ts=1$. Thus $P$ is a direct summand $eA_n$ of the right regular module for an idempotent $e$ (a right-module endomorphism of $A_n$ is left multiplication by its value at $1$). The cover is indecomposable: a nonzero decomposition would give a proper summand surjecting onto $L$, contrary to the superfluous kernel. [F3, given, choose, construct, algebra]

2.1 If $S$ is any simple right module and $h:P\to S$ is nonzero, then its kernel is maximal. Superfluity of $\ker\pi$ implies $\ker\pi\subseteq\ker h$: otherwise their sum is $P$ and the superfluity condition would force $\ker h=P$. Thus $h$ factors through $L$. By [F1] and [F5], $\dim\operatorname{Hom}_{A_n}(eA_n,S)$ is $1$ for $S=L$ and $0$ otherwise. Evaluation at $e$ identifies this Hom space with $Se$: the inverse sends $v\in Se$ to the map $ea\mapsto va$. Hence $\dim Se$ has those same values. This also proves any finite-dimensional projective module surjecting onto $L$ contains $P$ as a summand, by repeating step 1.1 with that module in place of $A_n$. Finally every indecomposable projective has a simple quotient, hence is the cover of that quotient by this summand assertion. [F1, F3, F5, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Left multiplication by $e$ is an exact functor on left modules: for an exact sequence, a lift of $ey$ can be replaced by $e$ times that lift. Apply it to the two-sided ideal filtration [F2]. The resulting filtration of $eA_n=P$ has layer $(eU_s)\otimes V_{n,s}$, a direct sum of $\dim eU_s$ copies of $V_{n,s}$. Every simple constituent of $U_s$ is the reflected left version of a simple constituent of $V_{n,s}$, because reflection is an exact equivalence. By the invariant quotient forms in [F1], that reflected simple is the ordinary left dual of the corresponding right simple $S$. Its $e$-image has dimension $\dim Se$, since $e$ acts by the transpose operator on the dual. Exactness and step 2.1 therefore give $\dim eU_s=[V_{n,s}:L_{n,p}]$. We have proved, without a semisimplicity or quasiheredity assumption, a standard filtration $[P_{n,p}:V_{n,s}]=[V_{n,s}:L_{n,p}].$ In particular its layer order is increasing defect number, equivalently decreasing arc count. [F1, F2, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 At a critical label, [F1] says the only standard containing $L_{n,p}$ is $V_{n,p}$, once. Step 3.1 gives $P_{n,p}\cong V_{n,p}$. The same argument applies to every label at $\kappa=1,\infty$. At a finite-order noncritical nonzero head, the standards containing it are $V_{n,p}$ and, when present, its neighbor on the lower-defect side, $V_{n,b}$ with $b=p+r$. This follows by solving the adjacent-reflection relation in [F1] in the reverse direction. If $k=0$, $n-2b+1=-r<0$ and $b$ is absent. If $k>0$, $n-2b=k\kappa-r-1\ge0$ and it is present. Each occurrence has multiplicity one. At $\kappa=2$, even rank, the possible $b=n/2$ is included because the zero-form standard is the actual simple $L_{n,n/2-1}$ by [F1]. Thus step 3.1 gives either $P_{n,p}=V_{n,p}$ or exactly the asserted two-standard filtration. Since $b>p$, its $V_{n,b}$ layer is a submodule and its $V_{n,p}$ layer the quotient, yielding the exact sequence. It is nonsplit: both standards are nonzero, whereas the cover in step 1.1 is indecomposable. [F1, step 1.1, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 For $k>0$, the starting label $(n-r,p)$ has defect number $k\kappa-1$ and is critical; its standard is projective by step 4.1. Induction preserves projectivity: the adjunction in [F4] identifies maps from an induced module with maps from the original module into a restriction, and restriction preserves surjections, so the defining lifting property is preserved. The $r$-fold induced module $Q$ is therefore projective. Repeatedly applying the standard induction sequences gives a filtration of $Q$ whose layers are quotients of the standards $V_{n,p+j}$, $0\le j\le r$, with multiplicities at most $\binom rj$. To justify this even though induction is only right exact, induct the existing filtration: the images of its submodules still form a filtration, and each new layer is a quotient of the induction of the old layer; the two-term sequence in [F4] refines these layers. No left-exactness is assumed. The exceptional induction input $(2,1,0)$ is never encountered: every intermediate defect is at least $k\kappa-1-(r-1)>0$. [F4, step 2.1, step 4.1, algebra]

6.1 On the standard indexed by $p+j$ the central eigenvalue is $q^{k\kappa+r-2j}+q^{-(k\kappa+r-2j)}$. It equals $f_{n,p}$ exactly when $j\equiv0$ or $j\equiv r\pmod\kappa$: use $x+x^{-1}=y+y^{-1}$ if and only if $(x-y)(x-y^{-1})=0$, and $q^{2k\kappa}=1$. Since $0\le j\le r<\kappa$, only $j=0,r$ qualify. Generalized eigenspaces of a central operator are submodules; the associated polynomial spectral projection is exact on finite-dimensional modules, as is seen by applying the same projection to a lift. Thus the $f_{n,p}$-space $Q_f$ is projective and step 5.1 bounds its dimension by $\dim V_{n,p}+\dim V_{n,p+r}$. Successive standard quotient maps give a surjection $Q\to V_{n,p}\to L_{n,p}$; its restriction to $Q_f$ remains onto, because the other generalized eigenspaces have distinct eigenvalues. Step 2.1 makes $P_{n,p}$ a direct summand of $Q_f$. Step 4.1 already gives $\dim P_{n,p}=\dim V_{n,p}+\dim V_{n,p+r}$, so the bound is saturated and $Q_f\cong P_{n,p}$, proving the stated realization. [F4, step 2.1, step 4.1, step 5.1, algebra]

7.1 At $\delta=0$, $\kappa=2$. Odd ranks have only critical labels and are covered by step 4.1. At rank $2m$, the simple labels are $0\le p<m$ by [F1]; each has $r=1$ and $k>0$. The repeated-induction realization in step 6.1 therefore has just one induction, from the odd-rank critical standard $V_{2m-1,p}$. Its two standard constituents both have eigenvalue $0$, so the entire induction is the selected generalized eigenspace. This proves the final displayed formulas and excludes a cover for the zero quotient label. At rank zero the algebra is $\mathbb C$, whose single simple regular module is projective. All covers and all exceptional cases have now been included. [F1, F4, step 4.1, step 6.1, algebra] ∎
